mastery.oneLine: Mobilization that uses joint shape (the convex-concave rule) to pick the glide direction, and traction grades to loosen, take up slack, or stretch.
mastery.whatItIs: The Kaltenborn-Evjenth approach explains which way a joint surface should glide so that a restricted movement can improve. You apply sustained or gentle traction and gliding in the joint's own 'treatment plane', using three stages that range from simply relieving pressure to stretching tight tissue.
mastery.analogy: A key only turns if you push it in the direction the lock expects. Joint surfaces are curved; if you know their shape, you know which way the bone must slide for the movement to open up.
coreIdeas: Convex-concave rule: when a convex surface moves on a concave one, the bone glides opposite to the direction the bone's shaft moves. When a concave surface moves on a convex one, the glide goes the same way as the shaft.
Three stages of traction: Stage I loosens (relieves pressure, no stretch), Stage II takes up the slack, Stage III stretches tissue.
Compare to the other side and feel the end-feel (the quality of the stop) to judge whether the joint is stiff, loose or normal.

terms.meaning: Convex is rounded outward like a ball; concave is curved inward like a cup.
An imaginary flat plane across the concave joint surface. Gliding runs parallel to it and traction runs at right angles to it.
The free play in tissues before they begin to tighten.
What the stop at the end of a movement feels like: firm, hard, springy or empty.
A joint that moves less than expected.

whenToUse: A joint that moves less than the other side with a firm, capsular-type end-feel.
When you need to decide glide direction logically, for example for shoulder elevation or knee extension.
Pain-dominant joints (Stage I) and stiff joints (Stage III) in the same framework.
whenNot: Unstable joints, acute fractures, active infection or inflammation, and suspected tumour.
Hypermobile joints, where you stabilize instead of stretching.
Any worsening neurological symptoms during the technique.

steps.title: Find the joint and its shape
steps.detail: Example: the shoulder. The humeral head is convex and the socket is concave.

steps.title: Work out the glide direction
steps.detail: For shoulder elevation, the convex head must glide downward (inferior), opposite to the arm rising. For knee extension, the concave tibia glides forward on the convex femur.

steps.title: Compare sides and feel the end-feel
steps.detail: Test the same glide on both joints. Note which is stiffer, and whether it is painful.

steps.title: Stage I
steps.detail: Apply a small traction that just relieves joint pressure. Use this to calm pain and test sensitivity.

steps.title: Stage II then III
steps.detail: Take up the slack, then add a sustained stretch into the resistance if the joint is not irritable.

steps.title: Release slowly and retest
steps.detail: Let go gradually and re-check the original movement.

mastery.dose: Typical teaching range: a gentle Stage I traction held about 10 seconds for pain; for stiffness, a Stage III stretch held roughly 6-10 seconds and released, repeated several times. Adjust to the response.

example.patient: Meena, 58, cannot lift her right arm above the shoulder after six weeks in a sling.
example.assessment: Elevation is 100 degrees on the right and 160 on the left, stopping with a firm end-feel. Pain is mild and settles quickly.
example.treatment: Using the convex-concave rule you apply an inferior glide of the humeral head with the arm supported, after a short Stage I traction to settle the joint, then a Stage III stretch.
example.reassess: Elevation reaches 120 degrees. You follow with active lifting practice with a stick, then repeat within a few days.

mistakes: Applying the glide in the wrong direction because the rule was memorized, not understood.
Stretching (Stage III) an irritable, painful joint.

selfTest.q: Concave tibia moves on a convex femur in knee extension. Which way does the tibia glide?
selfTest.a: Forward, in the same direction as the shaft moves.

selfTest.q: What is Stage I traction for?
selfTest.a: To relieve pressure and settle pain, with no stretch.

mastery.recap: Know the joint shape, choose the glide direction, escalate the stage only if the joint is calm.
mastery.evidence: The convex-concave rule is a useful teaching model, but real joints do not always glide exactly as predicted. Evidence for outcomes is similar to other mobilization: helpful short-term for selected patients, best with exercise.

depth.why: The convex-concave rule predicts the direction of the accessory glide: a convex surface moving on a concave one glides opposite to the bone's movement, a concave on a convex glides in the same direction. Grade I (loosening) unloads the joint, grade II takes up the slack, grade III stretches the capsule. Traction is the safest first move because it reduces compression and pain while testing the capsule.
choose: Use grade I traction for pain and to test irritability; grade II to assess and take up slack; grade III only when the capsular pattern is non-irritable.
Prefer it when you need a reasoned direction for each joint (the rule) rather than an oscillation tolerance.
Prefer Maitland when pain modulation with oscillations is the goal and the direction is less important.
parameters: small distraction that only neutralises joint pressure, 7-10 s with rest, a few repetitions
distraction that takes up the slack, 7-10 s, 3-6 repetitions
distraction or glide that stretches the capsule, sustained 7-10 s then release, 3-6 repetitions
a plane perpendicular to the line from the axis of rotation to the centre of the concave surface
depth.progress: Move from grade I to II to III as irritability settles; add active movement and loaded range once the passive range is available.
measure: Capsular pattern ratio of the restricted movements
Active range and a functional task
Pain response during the grade, not only after it
depth.evidence: The rule describes joint mechanics well in vitro, but in real patients the segment may not behave exactly to it. Clinical trials support mobilisation as a component of care; the rule itself is a clinical guide rather than a proven determinant of outcome.
pitfalls: Applying the rule to a joint with a surgical or traumatic change in shape.
Taking the slack out and holding without feeling the end-feel change.
Skipping the plane: a glide off the treatment plane compresses instead of gliding.

heading.en: The three traction grades and the glide

intro.en: Traction is a pull that separates the joint surfaces; the glide slides one surface along the other. The grade says how much load.
intro.ur: Traction woh khinchao hai jo joint surfaces ko alag karta hai; glide ek surface ko doosri ke saath slide karta hai. Grade batata hai kitna load.

what.en: A very small pull that cancels the normal pressure between the joint surfaces. No stretch. Used for pain.
what.ur: Bohat chhota khinchao jo joint surfaces ke beech normal pressure khatam karta hai. Stretch nahi. Dard ke liye.

en: Position the joint in resting position.
ur: Joint ko resting position mein rakhein.
Narmi se hold ya oscillate karein.

what.en: Pulls until the slack in the capsule and surrounding tissue is taken up. The first sense of resistance.
what.ur: Tab tak khinchta hai jab tak capsule aur aas paas ke tissue ki slack khatam na ho. Pehli resistance mehsoos hoti hai.

en: Add pull until you feel the slack come out.
Hold for a few seconds, then ease.
ur: Khinchao barhayein jab tak slack nikalti mehsoos ho.
Kuch second hold karein, phir narm karein.

tag.ur: Tight tissue ko stretch karta hai

what.en: Pulls beyond the slack to stretch the tight capsule and ligaments. Used for stiffness.
what.ur: Slack se aagay kheench kar tight capsule aur ligaments ko stretch karta hai. Stiffness ke liye.

en: Hold for a short time and retest.
ur: Thori der hold karein aur retest karein.

tag.en: Slides one surface along the other
tag.ur: Ek surface ko doosri par slide

what.en: A slide of one joint surface along the other, in the direction the joint shape suggests, to restore gliding.
what.ur: Ek joint surface ka doosri par slide, us direction mein jo joint ki shape batati hai, glide wapas laane ke liye.

en: Take up the slack with traction.
Glide the other bone in the treatment direction.
ur: Doosri bone ko treatment direction mein glide karein.

urdu.short: Kaltenborn–Evjenth approach mein joint par sustained traction ya glide diya jata hai. Is mein therapist joint ki position aur treatment plane ko madde-nazar rakhta hai. Force aur grade ka intikhab patient ke symptoms, tissue response aur reassessment ke mutabiq hota hai—sirf mechanical model ki bunyaad par nahi.

details.heading: Yeh approach kya hai?
details.text: Is approach ka focus joint ki chhoti translatoric movements par hai, jaise traction aur glide. Traction mein joint surfaces ko ek doosray se door ki taraf load diya jata hai; glide mein ek joint surface doosri ke muqablay mein slide karti hai. Patient ko aaram-deh position mein rakhna aur relevant segment ko stabilize karna technique ka aham hissa hai.

details.heading: Traction grades ka matlab
details.text: Grade I ko joint compression ko neutralize karne, Grade II ko slack take-up karne, aur Grade III ko restricted periarticular tissues par stretch dene ke liye describe kiya jata hai. Yeh teaching framework hai; har patient ko Grade III ya strong stretch ki zaroorat nahi hoti. Pain, irritability, medical history aur safety ko pehle samjhein.

details.heading: Treatment plane aur glide
details.text: Treatment plane joint surface ki anatomy ke mutabiq define kiya jata hai. Classical convex–concave rule glide ki direction plan karne mein madad de sakta hai, lekin isay har joint aur har patient par baghair assessment ke apply nahi karna chahiye. Technique ke baad range, symptoms aur relevant function dobara check karein.

details.heading: Misal — sirf samjhane ke liye
details.text: Farz karein kisi patient ko wrist movement mein stiffness mehsoos hoti hai. Assessment ke baad therapist low-force traction ya glide ka short trial choose kar sakta hai aur phir wrist movement dobara check kar sakta hai. Yeh sirf concept samjhane ki fictional misal hai; har wrist problem ke liye yahi technique ya dose recommend nahi ki ja rahi.

details.heading: Safety aur yaad-dasht
details.text: Recent trauma, fracture ka shak, instability, active infection, severe unexplained pain ya neurological deterioration mein routine mobilization munasib nahi ho sakti. Osteoporosis, postoperative restrictions aur inflammatory flare mein extra ehtiyat chahiye. Agar response faida-mand na ho ya symptoms barhein, force ko barhane ke bajaye assessment aur plan par dobara ghour karein.

deeper.heading: Clinical reasoning
deeper.text: Sab se pehle samjhein ke limitation dard ki wajah se hai ya joint ki movement restricted hai. Relevant movement aur accessory glide ka assessment karein. Sirf joint tight lagne par mobilization select na karein; history, irritability, safety screening aur comparable movement ko saath rakhein. Treatment ke baad wohi movement dobara check karein.

deeper.heading: Application ko samjhein
deeper.text: Kaltenborn approach mein sustained glide aur traction ki direction aur grade important hotay hain. Grade tissue resistance, symptoms aur treatment goal ke mutabiq chuna jata hai. Contact aur stabilization clear hon, taake force intended joint tak pohanchay. Exact joint-specific hand placement practical supervised training se seekhein.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur reassessment
deeper.text: Aam ghalti hai zyada force lagana magar baseline record na karna. Har set ke baad pain, range aur function compare karein. Agar improvement na ho ya symptoms worsen hon, force barhane ke bajaye direction, dose ya overall plan reconsider karein.

deeper.heading: Evidence aur limits
deeper.text: Is technique ko guaranteed correction ya har stiffness ka hal na kahein. Response patient aur condition ke mutabiq vary karta hai. English chapter ki evidence limitations ko patient education mein bhi honestly reflect karein.

cue.wake: The convex-concave rule is a map—not a boss giving orders to every joint.
cue.question: If a textbook glide makes the patient's movement worse, who wins: the book or the patient?
cue.answer: The patient's safe response. Stop, reassess, and change the trial.
cue.easy: Translatoric glide = a small sliding movement of one joint surface relative to another.
cue.remember: Map, glide, check. Never force the map.

technique.storyHeadline: A joint can feel restricted. Which direction deserves your attention?

episode.patient: A painter struggles to reach above shoulder height. The arm moves, then hesitates. A joint-surface diagram might suggest one glide, but the patient's pain, irritability and functional goal are much more interesting than memorizing the arrow in that diagram.
episode.decision: You consider the joint's treatment plane and the purpose of traction or a translatoric glide. With support and a clear baseline, you test an appropriate direction. If discomfort increases, you do not defend the diagram—you change course.
episode.retest: You ask for the same overhead reach. Better tolerance may support continuing. If the arm still refuses the job, the correct textbook direction has not earned a permanent place in the plan.
episode.spark: The anatomy diagram is a map. The patient is the GPS.

aha.hook: Joint surfaces never studied the convex–concave rule.
aha.analogy: The treatment plane is your map, not your autopilot. Traction and glide help you navigate, but the patient tells you whether you are heading in the right direction.
aha.challenge: A glide follows the textbook direction perfectly, but the task remains painful. What wins: the diagram or the reassessment?
aha.reveal: The reassessment. The model informs a safe trial; it cannot substitute for a useful clinical change.

weave.dialogue: Patient: 'Why does the joint need a sideways movement when I want to lift my arm upward?' Clinician: 'Because the big movement includes smaller joint-surface motions. But our diagram is only a starting hypothesis.'
weave.watch: Imagine the arm fully supported while one hand stabilizes and the other introduces a measured glide. Nothing jerks; nothing needs to pop. The therapist asks about the familiar reach and watches the patient test it rather than admiring the neatness of the glide.
weave.method: Convex–concave principles help choose an initial direction, but they are not a GPS that shouts 'recalculating' whenever the patient disagrees. Anatomy, comfort, symptom behavior and clinical objective refine the trial.
weave.science: A joint is not two billiard balls rolling in an empty room: capsule, cartilage, muscles and neural responses all matter. The selected translatoric force is a controlled input, not visual proof of a particular hidden joint-surface correction.
weave.question: The glide follows the textbook perfectly but the functional reach worsens. Is the treatment still correct?
weave.answer: No meaningful positive response has been demonstrated. Stop or modify, assess symptom irritability, and use the patient's response rather than treating a model as a verdict.
weave.closer: The treatment plane is the map. Reassessment is the destination.

patientPosition: Support the joint in its resting or treatment position so surrounding muscles are relaxed.
Use belts, towels or the table when appropriate to reduce the amount of muscular effort needed from the therapist and patient.
therapistPosition: Stand in the line of the treatment plane and keep your body close to the patient.
Use a stable base of support so you can maintain a sustained force without shaking or changing direction.
handPlacement: Stabilize one bone firmly but comfortably.
Contact the moving bone close to the joint line using a broad surface of the hand or a treatment belt when appropriate.
Keep pressure away from superficial nerves and painful bony points.
forceDirection: Traction is applied perpendicular to the treatment plane.
Gliding is applied parallel to the treatment plane.
Grade I is a very small distraction that reduces compressive contact; Grade II takes up slack; Grade III stretches restricted periarticular tissue.
Convex-concave rules can guide the first choice of glide, but the patient's response confirms whether the direction is useful.
applicationSteps: 1. Measure active movement, passive movement, end feel and joint play.
2. Place the joint in a comfortable treatment position.
3. Stabilize the proximal segment and gently remove slack.
4. Apply Grade I or II first when pain is dominant; use Grade III only when stiffness is dominant and the joint is safe.
5. Hold the translatoric force steadily without bouncing.
6. Release slowly, allow a short rest, then reassess range and symptoms.
7. Repeat only if the response is positive and then reinforce the improvement with active movement.
expectedResponse: Reduced compression pain, improved joint play, easier osteokinematic movement, or a more comfortable end range.
stopCriteria: Sharp joint pain, apprehension, neurological symptoms, increasing guarding, or worsening movement after each attempt.
commonMistakes: Confusing osteokinematic motion with translatoric glide.
Applying traction in the wrong direction relative to the treatment plane.
Using Grade III in an acutely irritable joint.
Holding the distal limb without adequately stabilizing the proximal bone.
clinicalExample: Example: limited ankle dorsiflexion after a healed sprain may respond to a sustained talocrural glide. Recheck the weight-bearing lunge immediately, then train calf strength and squat/step mechanics.

mechanism.mechanismMap: Sustained traction/glide → reduced compression + mechanoreceptor input + tissue loading → pain modulation + increased movement tolerance → active use
mechanism.simpleExplanation: Kaltenborn mobilization uses sustained traction or translatoric gliding. The force can temporarily reduce joint compression, load the capsule in a controlled direction and provide strong sensory input. The likely result is a combination of pain modulation, reduced guarding and improved tolerance to movement rather than a permanent change in bone position.
stepByStep: 1. Traction or glide changes the mechanical load across the joint.
2. Capsule, ligament, muscle and skin receptors respond to the sustained force.
3. Low-grade traction may decrease compressive stress and make the joint feel more comfortable.
4. Higher-grade sustained loading can increase short-term extensibility and stretch tolerance of periarticular tissues.
5. Sensory input can change spinal and supraspinal pain processing.
6. Reduced pain/guarding allows more active range and better movement confidence.
7. Exercise consolidates the gained range and makes it functionally useful.
physiology: Joint distraction may transiently reduce articular compression and nociceptive input in compression-sensitive presentations.
Sustained tissue loading produces viscoelastic deformation and changes in stretch tolerance, although these changes are often temporary.
Mechanoreceptor input from joint and periarticular tissues can alter nociceptive processing.
Muscle tone may change through altered sensory input and reduced protective response.
There is no strong evidence that a single sustained glide permanently changes joint alignment.
clinicalTranslation: Grade I is mainly a comfort/compression-reduction strategy.
Grade II takes up slack and is commonly used to assess/treat pain without aggressive stretch.
Grade III provides greater capsular loading when stiffness is the main problem.
myths: Convex-concave rules are a useful starting model, not proof that one glide must work.
Traction does not 'open the joint permanently'.
More force does not automatically produce more mobility.
mechanism.evidenceNote: The mechanical model is useful clinically, but contemporary evidence suggests the response is multifactorial and includes neurophysiological as well as mechanical effects.

mechanismEvidence.summary: Manual therapy does not have one universal mechanism. Modern evidence supports interacting peripheral, spinal, supraspinal, neurovascular, neuromuscular and contextual responses. The exact mechanism responsible for a patient's clinical improvement is often uncertain.
mechanismEvidence.sourceTitle: The mechanisms of manual therapy: A living review of systematic, narrative, and scoping reviews

room.arrival: An overhead reach stops halfway. The patient looks at the arm as if it betrayed them. You observe the shoulder hike, then check the painful direction before considering the treatment plane.
room.touch: Stabilize comfortably and introduce a measured traction or translatoric glide chosen from anatomy and examination. A diagram suggests a direction; the patient's response decides whether to keep it.
room.retest: Repeat the reach without your hands. The real goal is easier function—not proving that a convex–concave rule is always the whole story.
